name: Rapid Prototyping

claims.claim_text: Shortening prototype turnaround does not simply save time; it resets what managers and customers expect of a design cycle, so the saved time is absorbed by additional requirements rather than banked. Faster tooling therefore tends to add scope to an electrical engineer's job rather than shrink it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've talked about that before, too, about just, like, the greater expectations and turnaround times. It's almost, you know, a curse. You know, it looks like a blessing up front, but it's actually a curse because now it's added requirements.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cultural Differences

claims.claim_text: Building a 3D model of the board and its enclosure before any hardware exists catches mechanical fit problems for free, which is why EDA packages added 3D mechanical views. An electrical engineer working this way is expected to do at least basic mechanical modelling and integrate it with the PCB.
claims.quote_verbatim: the individual designer is expected to be able to be, you know, to at least be able to do basic level mechanical stuff and integrate it with the PCB. And you do your 3D model before you even make it. Does your board fit in?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cultural Differences

claims.claim_text: Printing enclosures in-house is a prototype and short-run technique only; the economics invert once quantity is involved, so a printed case is a placeholder for a moulded one rather than a substitute.
claims.quote_verbatim: just for prototypes and short runs and things like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Otiose Ontocyclic Opiniasters

claims.claim_text: Because every design starts with incomplete information, pushing an imperfect version out and learning from it usually beats extending the design phase. The exception is a product with a single high-stakes introduction, where there is no second chance to correct in public.
claims.quote_verbatim: everybody has limited information when they start out with the design. Yeah. But, you know, you do the best you can. But eventually you got to push something out there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Yonderly Yodeling Yobbos

claims.claim_text: A one-shot consumer launch removes the option of iterating in the market, so the first release has to be both fast and correct; that constraint does not apply to most other hardware, where later revisions can absorb mistakes.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing a huge consumer product where you get one introduction, well, you have to be fast and awesome, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Yonderly Yodeling Yobbos

claims.claim_text: Physical access to a components market changes prototyping behaviour for parts whose selection depends on feel and size, such as switches, because holding candidates gives a sense of proportion that a catalogue page cannot. Ordering the same parts by mail forces buying roughly twenty of a switch just to find the one that is right.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really great for going down and, and holding stuff in your hands and getting like a real sense of the sizing on stuff
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Prototype turn time is bought, not given: the choices are a local board house at a premium, a distant one that costs schedule, or expedited shipping. Building prototypes close to home is standard advice because speed dominates every other consideration at the prototype stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're either going to find someone who does it close to home and pay the price in terms of management yelling at you, or you're going to pay through the nose for farming it out to someone close to home, or pay through the nose to get it shipped to you really, really quickly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: When a board can be respun in a couple of days, the cost of an individual layout mistake collapses and designers stop treating each spin as precious. Commodity PCB pricing and turn time, not any change in design skill, are what make that posture rational.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, I can re-spin in a couple of days if it's wrong, you know, who cares.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: For a complex instrument whose workflow is unproven, printing full-scale shells of every external component and staging them in a mock lab produces a testable workflow in very little time, with none of the internal engineering built.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually built in very little time a replica lab that looks like it has this technology installed and it has the workflow set up as a model example
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: A prototype in which every interaction is faked behind the scenes still yields valid workflow data, because the customer operating it cannot distinguish the mock from a working unit and behaves as they would with the real device.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there's like a man behind the curtain. It's a sample lab. So whatever – no matter what you do with the shell, you see the same images on the screen and whatever. But it's a demo. So the customer doesn't know that it doesn't work.
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: A mocked-up prototype is a variable experiment rather than a fixed demo: price, configuration and workflow difficulty can be changed between customer sessions, so each session tests a different hypothesis at no fabrication cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time you bring a customer in, you can change the experiment. So you can offer it at a different price point. You can change the configuration to make the workflow easier or harder.
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: The lever that gets a minimum viable product to market faster is cutting the requirements list, not working the existing requirements faster, which is why the specification document is where a prototyping effort should be aimed.
claims.quote_verbatim: The way we get the MVP to get to market a lot faster is by making the specification document easier by reducing the requirements.
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: A conference badge went from design through manufacturing in about eight weeks, showing that compressed hardware schedules are achievable when scope is fixed and the design is simple.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was making a badge for a conference. And it was like a ridiculous thing that I put together in like eight weeks, including design and manufacturing.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Validating only two or three prototype units before releasing a design to volume production is not enough to expose marginal component values; in one badge run, thirty to forty percent of units coming off the line failed and the factory had to stop the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: you know, I tested two or three units before it hit the factory. And they were coming off the line in the factory and like a good 30 or 40% of them weren't working.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Suboptimal crystal load capacitors are a classic marginal fault: a small handful of prototypes will start reliably while a large production population will not, so oscillator load capacitance deserves explicit verification rather than a pass on a few working boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had figured out that I – that my load caps on the crystal were suboptimal
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Some layout tools let a placed component instance have its pads edited without touching the library part, which is fast when a nearly-right footprint has to be fudged onto a prototype by enlarging a hole or a pad.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you decide, oh, you know, I'm just going to try to fudge this component in there and I've got this footprint that's kind of close. I can just increase the size of a hole or make a pad bigger without having to edit the library
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: The hazard of editing pads on a placed instance is that the board no longer matches the known-good library footprint, so the association between verified library part and fabricated copper is silently lost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can lose the association between the footprint that you've got in your library, which is maybe known good and what you actually spit out on the board
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: Proprietary connector ecosystems tax prototyping directly: a plain push button carrying the vendor's end plug sold for around eighteen to twenty dollars, which was enough to justify having a mould made for the connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like if you want to buy a touch sensor, which is just a button, it's a push button with their end plug on it. That's something like 18 or $20.
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A complete one-off prototype can be assembled by exporting the board's 3D view into a mechanical modelling tool, designing the case around it, and printing that case, with a cheap pooled-service PCB underneath. The result is unlikely to look finished but can come in under about a hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could, in theory, you know, if you got your boards printed by, like, the Dorkbot PDX guys, you know, for, you know, a cheap board with cheap parts on it and then you 3D printed your actual mechanical segment, I'm guessing you could probably make an entire prototype for less than 100 bucks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: Commercial desktop circuit board mills cost about five thousand dollars for a machine that is neither fast nor especially precise, which is what motivated a wave of open replacement designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's $5,000 for not a very fast machine with high precision but not very high precision
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Additive prototyping machines exert essentially no cutting force, so an extremely floppy and mechanically poor frame still produces a part, whereas a subtractive machine with the same frame stalls or crashes into the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: prototyping machines is that they have no cutting force. So you can have, like, the floppiest, crappiest mechanical machine in it. And it'll still print something.
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: A maximum power point tracker for satellite solar cells went from concept to fabricated PCB to integration in two flight vehicles in about three weeks, which is the pace an agile aerospace programme can sustain when it accepts flight risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: we shipped these two boards that were a concept three weeks before were integrated into a satellite and going to space in like three weeks
claims.speaker: Shaun Meehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: New hardware is flown on two vehicles rather than one so that losing contact with a single unit does not destroy the experiment; redundancy at the vehicle level is what makes flying an unproven board acceptable.
claims.quote_verbatim: You always want to put something into two satellites just in case something goes wrong and you can't contact one of them.
claims.speaker: Shaun Meehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: After a launch vehicle carrying their payloads exploded, a satellite team rebuilt and prototyped replacement hardware in nine days to make the next rocket, which stands as a documented upper bound on how fast flight hardware can be reconstituted.
claims.quote_verbatim: we talked about how basically their experiments were on the Antares rocket. And then that blew up. Right. And then basically they got on the SpaceX rocket nine days later.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Board turn time is a purchasable parameter with a wide price spread: a pooled low-cost service returns boards in roughly one to two weeks, while a domestic quick-turn house charges on the order of five to seven hundred dollars for overnight or two-day delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I'm doing my own stuff, more hobby type stuff or low priority for my business, then I'll go through OSH Park and get boards in a week or so or maybe two weeks. If I, on the other hand, for some of my higher priority stuff, I'll go through a company called Sunstone over in Portland and I'll pay, you know, I'll pay $500 or $700 and get, you know, overnight or two day turnaround.
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: A prototype is not finished when the board works, because documentation and host software are part of what a user needs; early adopters tolerate gaps but mainstream users do not, and each point of friction costs roughly thirty percent of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get those first adopters to use it. But, you know, if you're if you're going toward the standard user, any like I said, any bump costs you 30 percent right there
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Reaching for whichever tool you are already fluent in is the right call when the goal is a demonstration rather than a product, because a crude prototype in front of someone communicates more than an optimised one that does not exist yet.
claims.quote_verbatim: you use the tool you're comfortable with to, you know, get something done quickly, even if it's some phony prototype
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Planning for multiple prototype spins up front removes the pressure to verify everything on the first board, so the first version can be committed rather than endlessly refined.
claims.quote_verbatim: look, we have time for prototypes. We're, we're planning on multiple prototypes. Just pull the trigger.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: Not every choice on a first prototype is equally reversible: architectural picks such as the microcontroller and its software ecosystem propagate through every later revision, while most of the rest of the board can be changed several revs in.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first version matters a lot because a lot of that stuff carries through to the end of a design
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: Etching a board at home was worth doing when the alternative quick-turn service in Australia charged around a hundred dollars, and the same reasoning stopped applying once that price fell to about twenty dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: boards, the quick batch boards you could actually get in Australia were like a hundred bucks, not 20 bucks
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: The deadline, not the cost, is often what drives a self-made board: having a weekend to finish something rules out any service whose turn time exceeds the schedule regardless of price.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would etch my own boards because like I had a weekend to complete something and I wanted to get it done right then
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Any design question that depends on how the thing feels in a user's hands cannot be settled from a schematic or a screen, so hands-on user experience testing is the specific need that forces a same-day physical prototype.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're designing something that you need to have some hands on user experience testing, the only way that you can do that is with rapid prototyping
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Before building a test rig, state exactly what the test is trying to learn and what will count as success and failure, then find the absolute minimum and fastest way to test that single theory rather than the version that also delivers the features you eventually want.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's so important to be very specific about what the aim of the test that we're about to perform is going to be. What we consider success, what we consider failure, what we're actually going to trial
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Constraining yourself to the simplest possible test tends to surface equipment repurposed far outside its intended use, and such improvised rigs can answer the question adequately; office-store inkjet printers served as the starting apparatus for a conductive-ink printing venture.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can start using things that were never, ever, ever meant for the purpose that you're using it for and find that it tests your theory just fine. And that's what we did at the very beginning with using those Canon printers from, from the office supply store.
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: A visual programming environment shows the result of a change instantly, which is what makes it useful for shaping an idea before committing to firmware; the work can then either stay in that environment or be rewritten and optimised in compiled code.
claims.quote_verbatim: what's cool about having a visual program for rapid prototyping is you could see the result instantly and then, you know, do some basic math on top of it to really kind of shape out what your idea is
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Timothy Lamb

claims.claim_text: High-level interpreted runtimes such as Lua virtual machines and Python are worth using to churn out proofs of concept quickly, but a design intended for production beyond a handful of units warrants being redone properly in a lower-level implementation.
claims.quote_verbatim: i prototype with a lot of like lua vms and you know python and stuff i love that because it allows me to really quickly churn out prototypes and proof of concept
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: Breadboarding and soldering quick prototypes at each step, then measuring connectivity, response time and range on real test clusters, verifies a system incrementally; a sixty-page specification written up front can mandate behaviour that turns out to be unimplementable.
claims.quote_verbatim: we do a lot of test driven hardware developments in which we just breadboard everything you know solder up like quick prototypes
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: Continuous hardware verification is preferable to a long written specification because implementation regularly reveals that the specified behaviour cannot actually be achieved.
claims.quote_verbatim: verification in hardware along the way is um i'm more believer of that kind of concept than just writing a 60 page document right that mandates how things should work but then you know when you get to implementation you might find that actually you can't really do that
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: A cast acrylic shell with a story attached is a demonstration of industrial design, not of a working product: such a mock-up contains no electronics, no firmware and no software, and presenting one as a finished product is how crowdfunded vapourware happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: They, they cast some acrylic and they told a story around it. Right. Which is a classic media lab, uh, lore. And there were, there were no electronics inside. There were no, there was no firmware written. There was no software.
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Laying out a grid of pilot holes across a structural part lets components be moved and re-screwed as the design settles, which matters most on early prototypes where proportions are still being guessed. Machining a single hole is unforgiving by comparison, since a misplaced one means remaking the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's nice for like early prototypes as well because it's hard to gauge proportions and it makes iterating really easily when you can just move stuff around
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Looking back at a product with five successive generations of microcontroller, the corrective judgment was that more prototypes and faster failure would have been better than the path actually taken.
claims.quote_verbatim: I should have been a little more fail forward fast. I should have prototyped a little more.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Putting the first crude units directly into the hands of people who are neither developers nor engineers exposes usability failures immediately; requiring a JTAG box to program a device is the kind of barrier that only shows up when a non-specialist tries to use it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first thing we did is we got them into people's hands. Of people who weren't our developers and engineers.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Interpreted on-target languages are productive precisely in the one-to-ten-unit regime where prototypes live, and are the wrong choice for runs of hundreds of thousands where the per-unit cost of the overhead dominates.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing a large scale thing where you're, you know, making thousands of something or hundreds of thousands of something, this isn't the right approach for you. But if you're doing prototyping, um, like lots of us in the hobbyists are doing, we're making like one to ten of it
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: An on-device interpreter prompt reached over a serial link can report its own pin mappings on request, removing datasheet lookups from the bring-up loop. This suits work where timing is not tight and the aim is to get something functioning quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't need a really tight timing for something and you're just trying to make things happen when they should happen. And you're just trying to get, you know, something hammered out really quick
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Keeping prototyping capability in-house is sometimes driven by intellectual property containment rather than turn time, since every external vendor in the loop is another place a design can leak.
claims.quote_verbatim: they want to do rapid prototyping, keep the IP in-house, everything, so that nothing leaks out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Nerds In A Corner

claims.claim_text: When there is no schedule for a full custom board, a working proof of concept can be assembled from an off-the-shelf development board, a small custom sensor board mated to its standard pinout, an existing screen module, and a printed case around the stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't have time to spin up all an entire new board, but you know, I took a dev board off the shelf. I made a sensor board that was custom for my application. Uh, there was a standard pin out on the, the dev board. I just hooked into that. I had a screen that hooked into that. And then I 3d printed a 3d design, 3d modeled a case around it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: A prototype assembled from stock modules can cost ten to twenty times what the same function would cost in a production design, and that premium is still the right trade when the deliverable is a demonstration that has to exist by a date.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was probably, I don't know, 10, 20 times what it would cost in a final, in a final version of it, but it worked out great for, for what I was talking about.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: Bare prototype PCB cost has fallen to a couple of dollars per board, and where printing is available at the cost of materials the consumables are negligible, so schedule pressure rather than parts cost is what now decides how a prototype is built.
claims.quote_verbatim: So in that case, like the, I think the PCB cost two bucks to, to make
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: The cost balance for one-off and ten-off builds has inverted: materials once rivalled the non-recurring engineering, but materials are now cheap while engineering effort remains expensive, which argues for spending money on parts to save engineering time.
claims.quote_verbatim: it used to be when you made one or 10 of things, the cost of the materials was as much as the cost of the NRE. But now the cost of material is, is so cheap and NREs is still expensive.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: Milling boards in-house is generally not worth it for high-complexity designs, but it is well suited to rapid iteration where the value is getting a physical board the same day; the trace fineness a skilled operator achieves on a mill is easy to underestimate until seen in person.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the times for like higher complexity boards, it's not really worth it, but I really like the rapid iteration type stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with MG (Mike Grover)

claims.claim_text: Reusing a part or subsystem you already know, even when it is neither the cheapest nor the technically best choice, is the correct move when speed is the binding constraint; a fully custom design is reserved for the piece that genuinely has to be custom.
claims.quote_verbatim: especially if you're going fast and that's kind of the thing that I've been running into more is just needing to go fast. It's like you just got to grab what's nearby and just get something working
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Rubber Ducking

claims.claim_text: Going from a printed pattern to a usable metal part is a large amount of additional work, and large parts must be printed in several pieces, which leaves a seam in the finished casting.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is a huge amount of work to go from a printed part to a part made out of metal that you can put in your car
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Keyzermas Vacation

claims.claim_text: Printing channels and filling them with conductive silver ink builds up a board layer by layer, which allows arbitrarily many layers to be produced with rapid iteration rather than a fabrication cycle per revision.
claims.quote_verbatim: essentially you're just doing, you know, many, many, many layers of PCBs. But you can do them obviously with, you know, rapid, rapid iteration.
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: The same motion hardware and control software used for printing circuits was repurposed for rapid prototyping of athletic footwear by swapping the deposited material to polyurethanes, showing that the machine platform is largely independent of the material chemistry.
claims.quote_verbatim: We use the same software to drive all the systems, but we swapped out all the materials for polyurethanes and used very similar processes to help bring in a rapid prototyping for athletic shoes
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Choosing a widely-supported development board form factor for a prototype lets existing compliant peripheral boards be stacked on without new hardware, and the software already written for those peripherals is reused as-is.
claims.quote_verbatim: because it's a feather form factor, any feather compliant, um, peripheral board could be stacked on there. So if people are accustomed to certain sensors that are feather compatible, they could just stack it up like a cake and reuse the software they may already have in place
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Removing the compile-upload-verify cycle changes the working loop to edit-and-save with the result visible live, which is a different development paradigm rather than a marginal speed-up of the same one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's no longer like, it's not click upload, verify test, whatever. It's literally like write code, hit save, write code, hit save. And like, you're just seeing this live action happen.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller with native USB removes the USB-to-UART converter from a prototype board entirely, cutting one part and its associated layout and driver problems from every early spin.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't need a USB to UR converter anymore, which is nice. Right. It actually is built in.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Histogrammic or Histomagraphical

claims.claim_text: Developing custom hardware for an application typically takes on the order of six to eight weeks plus substantial engineering effort before anything exists to test, which is the argument for starting on a development kit carrying every connector the eventual system needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: before they have a hardware this takes around six to eight weeks or something like this and also a lot of engineering effort at this point so why don't start with i would say a dev kit
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz
claims.episode_title: Vapor Phase with Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: Development kits stop being the right answer once volumes rise, and the custom engineering effort to productise a module-based design is on the order of fifteen to twenty-five thousand in euros or dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: a custom engineering effort for jets nvidia is around 15 to 25 000 euros for or dollars for bringing the product out
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz
claims.episode_title: Vapor Phase with Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: In-house fabrication compresses the mechanical iteration loop to roughly ten iterations in a single day, against a loop measured in shipping cycles when the part is made elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I can get probably 10 iterations in a day versus, you know, any kind of shipping back and forth, that sort of thing.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gremlins in the machine

claims.claim_text: A prototyping board can be fabricated as a blank template covered in a regular cross pattern of vias, so that circuits are assembled onto a stock substrate instead of waiting for a custom board on every iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: he made a PCB that's, like, the board itself is made to, as, like, a template for stuff. So, you already have, like, this kind of cross pattern of vias that are already there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tugging on the Nerd Heartstring

claims.claim_text: Owning desktop placement capability down to 0402 parts does not by itself close the prototyping loop, because a board still has to be obtained, which leaves milling or an outside fab as the remaining bottleneck.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have this pick and place. It's great. But you have to still, like, get a board.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tugging on the Nerd Heartstring

claims.claim_text: Cheap printing and quick-turn boards make it easy to spin hardware fast, but speed creates its own failure mode: finishing with something that does about eighty percent of what was promised is not a deliverable.
claims.quote_verbatim: The thing is you don't want your win to be 80% of what you actually need to deliver it to be used.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Fitting ordinary square header pins to a module and sliding the mating board onto them gives a friction-fit connection with no soldering, so modules can be added and removed freely while a prototype is still changing.
claims.quote_verbatim: You just put the regular stabby steak pins on it, on your board and you can just slide it on and it's going to make contact
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Once the arrangement is settled, the pins are left unpopulated and the module is reflowed directly onto the baseboard; for that to work the baseboard's through-holes should be replaced with surface pads that will take solder paste.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the next round, don't populate the stabby things. Just, just a reflow directly on, on, on top of that. You know, you probably want to replace your, your baseboard, you know, through holes with just, you know, pads, surface pads
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner
